opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest thing it did was give me a really long runway of being obsessed with one question. When you decide at fourteen that this is the thing you want to work on, you don't have a career plan or a sense of what's prestigious. You just have this almost naive conviction that building intelligence is the most important problem there is, and you start pulling on every thread you can find.

I didn't have a formal path into it at that age, so a lot of it was self-directed: reading whatever I could get my hands on, writing code, trying to reimplement things from papers, and failing a lot. That shaped me in a couple of ways. One, I got very comfortable with not knowing things and just figuring them out from first principles, because there wasn't anyone handing me a curriculum. Two, I developed a bias toward building rather than just reading. You learn really quickly that an idea that sounds beautiful on paper often falls apart the moment you actually run it, and that feedback loop became how I think about research in general.

The other thing is that committing early means you're making decisions with a much longer time horizon than most people. Some of the things I spent years on as a teenager didn't pay off directly, but they built intuition. When I later got into more serious research, things like reinforcement learning and game-theoretic settings, I already had this backlog of half-formed ideas and failed experiments to draw from. So in a weird way, being young and stubborn about it was an advantage. I didn't know enough to think it was unrealistic, and by the time I did, I was already too deep in to stop.

r001.rationale: The response says starting at fourteen gave him a long runway for self-directed learning and experimentation, but it does not say this enabled him to pursue opportunities earlier than he otherwise would have.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest thing it did was remove the question of "what should I do with my life" from the table very early. When you're fourteen and you decide this is the thing, you stop spending energy on the search and start spending all of it on the work. That compounds. I had years of just reading papers, implementing things, failing, before I was anywhere near a job or a lab.

The second thing is that I had no credentials and no permission, so I had to learn to teach myself. I couldn't take a course on deep learning at that age, so I'd read the textbook, get stuck, go back to the math, come back. That built a kind of stubbornness that I think is actually the core skill in research. Most of research is being confused for a long time and not quitting.

And then there's a flip side, which is that I made every mistake you can make. I spent months on ideas that were obviously bad in hindsight because I didn't have anyone telling me they were bad. But I think that's underrated. You develop taste by having been wrong a lot and feeling it, not by being told what's right. By the time I was working on things like poker AI with Noam and the people at Facebook, I had a pretty strong internal sense of what was likely to work, and that sense came from all those years of being alone with the problem.

The last thing I'd say is it made the whole thing feel personal rather than professional. It's never been a career for me. It's the thing I decided to do as a kid, and I'm still doing it.

r002.rationale: The response mentions later work with Noam, but does not say that being a decent teenage researcher was enough to attract a strong mentor.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest effect was that it gave me a lot of time to explore. At fourteen, you don’t need to have a polished research agenda. You can follow your curiosity, try to build something, get stuck, and then learn whatever you need to make progress. That cycle is a really good way to develop as a researcher.

Having a direction also made learning feel purposeful. Math and programming became tools for answering questions I cared about. But I’d distinguish committing to AI from committing to a particular idea about AI. The first gives you persistence; you still want to be very willing to change your mind about the second.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest effect was that it gave me a lot of time to explore. At fourteen, you don’t have the same pressure to produce something immediately useful, so you can follow your curiosity, try things, and get stuck. You learn how to learn independently.

It also meant that, over time, the technical foundations became more intuitive. But I wouldn’t say starting early automatically makes you a better researcher. What matters is spending time on difficult problems, questioning your assumptions, and being willing to change your mind.
